_about: Contrastive stress set for résumé-interview answer evaluators. Labels are Claude-authored (annotator 'claude'), written BEFORE any evaluator was run, on the 0-4 tier scale: 0 worthless/non-answer, 1 poor, 2 partial, 3 good, 4 excellent. Lengths are deliberately varied within each tier so answer length cannot predict the label.

chronos.title: Chronos - Distributed Task Orchestration System
chronos.summary: Built a distributed task orchestration system using FastAPI, PostgreSQL, RabbitMQ and Redis, supporting dependency-aware workflows, asynchronous execution and concurrency-safe task claiming. Implemented a transactional outbox, lease-based execution with heartbeats, automatic retries, crash recovery through lease reaping, and Redis-backed rate limiting.

securelogin.title: Secure Login Service

items.question: Why did you use a transactional outbox in Chronos instead of publishing to RabbitMQ directly?

answers.why: Names the dual-write problem precisely, explains the mechanism in their stack, and the cost they accepted.
answers.answer: The problem was the dual write. When a task finished I had to update its row in Postgres and also publish the next tasks to RabbitMQ, and if the process died between those two, either the DB said done but nothing downstream ran, or a message went out for a state change that rolled back. So I write the outbox row in the same Postgres transaction as the state change, and a separate relay process polls the outbox and publishes. The trade-off is at-least-once delivery, so I made the consumers idempotent by checking the task's state version before acting, and there's a little extra latency from the relay polling interval, which was about 200 milliseconds.

answers.why: Brief but exactly right: atomicity with the DB write, relay, idempotent consumers.
answers.answer: So the state change and the event commit atomically in one Postgres transaction. The relay publishes afterwards, and consumers are idempotent because it's at-least-once.

answers.why: Correct core idea but no mechanism or trade-offs; honest about the gap.
answers.answer: Mainly to avoid losing messages if the worker crashed. I read about the pattern and it seemed like the safe way to do it. I'm honestly not fully sure about all the edge cases with it, I mostly got it working and tested crashing the worker.

answers.why: Textbook definition of the pattern, nothing about Chronos or their decisions.
answers.answer: The transactional outbox pattern is a well-known microservices pattern used to reliably publish events. Instead of sending a message directly to a broker, the service writes the event to an outbox table as part of its local database transaction, and a separate process reads from the outbox and publishes the messages. This ensures consistency between the database and the message broker and is widely used in event-driven architectures.

answers.why: Confident but false: an outbox does not give exactly-once delivery, and RabbitMQ does not require it for ordering.
answers.answer: I used the outbox because RabbitMQ on its own can't guarantee ordering, and the outbox table gives you exactly-once delivery end to end, so every task is guaranteed to run one time only, which meant I didn't need to worry about idempotency or duplicate handling anywhere in the workers. It basically makes the whole system transactional across Postgres and RabbitMQ.

answers.why: Strings together resume terms with no causal explanation of the outbox decision.
answers.answer: Chronos used FastAPI, PostgreSQL, RabbitMQ and Redis, with leases and heartbeats and retries and rate limiting, and the outbox was part of making all of that reliable and scalable for the workflows.

answers.why: Answer centres on Kafka and Debezium, which aren't part of this project; contradicts the resume.
answers.answer: Honestly the main reason was that I used Debezium change data capture on the outbox table to stream into Kafka, so Kafka handled the ordering for me and the consumers just read the topic.

answers.why: No content.
answers.answer: I don't really remember why, it was a while ago.

answers.why: Short and wrong reason (outbox has nothing to do with speed).
answers.answer: Because it made publishing faster.

items.question: How did you structure the detection pipeline in AI SOC Analyst?

answers.why: Clear stages, deterministic detection vs LLM narration split, concrete rule example and reason.
answers.answer: Logs come in as Windows event logs, Linux auth logs or CSV, and the first stage normalises them into one event schema with timestamp, user, source IP, host and event type. Then detection is deterministic rules, not the LLM: for example password spraying is one source IP failing logins against more than ten distinct users inside five minutes, and brute force is many failures against one user. Only after a rule fires does the LangGraph flow kick in, where Gemini gets the matched events and writes the incident report and timeline. I kept the LLM out of detection because I didn't want it hallucinating an attack, it only explains what the rules already found.

answers.answer: There's a parsing step for the different log types, and then the agent looks at them and figures out if there's an attack like brute force. I think the detection part could be better, right now a lot of it depends on the model's judgment.

items.question: How did you make redirects fast in ShortHop?

answers.why: Cache-aside explained with miss path, TTL, invalidation and a measured result; analytics kept off the hot path.
answers.answer: The redirect path checks Redis first with the short code as the key. On a hit it returns the 302 straight away, and on a miss it reads Mongo, writes the mapping into Redis with a 24 hour TTL and then redirects, so popular links basically never touch Mongo. I measured p50 going from about 15 milliseconds to under one. The other thing was I moved click analytics off the request path, the redirect just pushes an event and returns, and the enrichment with GeoIP happens asynchronously, otherwise the analytics would have slowed every redirect.

answers.why: Brief but correct and specific.
answers.answer: Cache-aside in Redis keyed by short code with a TTL, and the analytics are written asynchronously so the redirect never waits on them.

answers.why: Right idea, little detail, no evidence of measuring.
answers.answer: I put Redis in front of the database so the redirects are cached. I didn't really benchmark it properly but it felt a lot faster after.

answers.why: Generic performance advice; nothing about what they did.
answers.answer: There are many ways to improve performance in web applications, such as caching frequently accessed data, using a CDN, optimising database queries with indexes, minimising payload sizes and using load balancers to distribute traffic across multiple servers. Caching is especially important for read-heavy workloads.

I also dropped MongoDB from the redirect path completely and made Redis the only store with persistence turned off, which is what made it so fast.

items.question: Why did you choose bcrypt for password storage in the Secure Login Service?

answers.why: Correct reasoning (slow, adaptive cost, built-in salt), alternatives weighed, a concrete parameter and its consequence.
answers.answer: Password hashes need to be slow so that if the database leaks, offline guessing is expensive. A fast hash like SHA-256 can do billions of guesses a second on a GPU. bcrypt has a tunable cost factor and generates and stores the salt inside the hash string, so I didn't have to manage salts myself. I picked cost 12, which was around 250 milliseconds a login on my machine, acceptable for users but painful for an attacker. I did look at Argon2 since it's memory-hard and the current recommendation, but the Python bcrypt library was simpler to deploy with Flask on the host I had, so I went with bcrypt.

answers.why: Short, correct core reasoning.
answers.answer: Because it's deliberately slow with a configurable cost and salts automatically, so leaked hashes are expensive to crack, unlike plain SHA-256.

answers.why: Correct-ish but shallow, honest about following advice.
answers.answer: Mostly because it's the standard recommendation for passwords and it handles the salt. I didn't compare it with the others in much depth.

answers.why: Generic security statement, no reasoning about the choice.
answers.answer: Security is very important in any authentication system. Storing passwords securely protects users' data and the company's reputation, and following best practices like hashing helps prevent breaches. It is important to always use well-established libraries rather than writing your own cryptography.

answers.why: Wrong: bcrypt is a hash, not encryption; it cannot be decrypted; and speed is not its advantage.
answers.answer: I chose bcrypt because it's the fastest encryption algorithm for passwords, so logins stay quick even under load, and because it's reversible with the server key, which meant we could decrypt and email users their password if they forgot it. That's much more user-friendly than forcing a reset.

items.question: What was the hardest bug you hit in the Kafka clickstream pipeline, and how did you fix it?

answers.why: Specific bug, diagnosis steps, root cause and fix in their stack.
answers.answer: Events were getting counted twice in SQLite after I restarted the consumer container. I added logging of partition and offset per event and saw the duplicates were always the last batch before the restart. The consumer was auto-committing offsets on a timer, but I was writing to SQLite after the commit point, so on a crash the batch had been processed but the offset was behind, and Kafka redelivered it. I turned off auto-commit, committed manually after the SQLite transaction succeeded, and made the insert idempotent with the event id as a unique key, so a redelivery just gets ignored.

answers.why: Concise but specific bug and correct fix.
answers.answer: Duplicate rows after consumer restarts. Auto-commit was committing offsets out of step with the SQLite writes, so I switched to manual commits after the write and made inserts idempotent on event id.

answers.why: Real bug, but vague diagnosis and an unexplained fix.
answers.answer: The consumer couldn't connect to Kafka when I ran it in Docker. It was some networking thing with the advertised listeners, I found a Stack Overflow answer and changed the config and it worked.

answers.why: Generic debugging philosophy, no actual bug.
answers.answer: Debugging distributed systems is always challenging because there are many moving parts. My approach is to reproduce the issue, read the logs carefully, isolate components and test hypotheses one at a time until I find the root cause, then write a fix and verify it.

answers.why: Root-cause claim is wrong: adding partitions doesn't fix duplicates; Kafka doesn't 'delete' after reading.
answers.answer: The hardest bug was messages disappearing, because Kafka deletes each message as soon as a consumer reads it, so when my second consumer started it had nothing to read. I fixed it by adding more partitions, which stops Kafka from deleting messages and also guarantees exactly-once processing across all the consumers.
